Branching directly from the aorta means the blood arrives at high pressure from the left ventricle, so it reaches the muscle quickly and in large volume.

questions.question: A change in which factor has the biggest effect on resistance? A blood pressure, B length of the blood vessel, C radius of the blood vessel lumen, D thickness of the blood vessel wall.
questions.answer: C radius of the blood vessel lumen.
steps: Poiseuille's relationship gives resistance proportional to length divided by the fourth power of radius.
Because radius is raised to the fourth power, a small change in radius causes a very large change in resistance.
Blood pressure does not change resistance, and length and wall thickness have much smaller effects.
Doubling the radius reduces resistance to one-sixteenth, so radius dominates.

questions.question: Explain how arteries are adapted to reduce resistance to blood flow.
questions.answer: Arteries have a wide lumen, which lowers resistance, and a smooth endothelial lining that reduces friction with the blood.
steps: Resistance falls sharply as the radius of the lumen increases, because it depends on radius to the fourth power.
Arteries have a wide lumen compared with arterioles and capillaries, giving low resistance for the blood flow.
The inner endothelium is smooth, which reduces friction between the blood and the vessel wall.
Elastic walls stretch and recoil, keeping blood pressure and flow steady.

questions.question: Explain how arteries are adapted to accommodate sudden increases in blood flow.
questions.answer: Arteries have elastic fibres in their walls, so they stretch to expand the lumen and absorb the extra volume, then recoil to keep blood moving.
steps: Arteries have many elastic fibres (elastin) in their walls.
When blood is pumped in suddenly, the elastic fibres stretch and the lumen expands.
This absorbs the extra volume and limits the rise in pressure.
Elastic recoil then pushes the blood on, keeping the flow steady between heartbeats.

questions.question: Explain why a reduction in the compliance of a blood vessel can lead to cardiovascular disease (CVD).
questions.answer: Stiffer arteries cannot expand, so systolic pressure rises and the heart works harder, damaging artery walls and promoting atherosclerosis, which leads to CVD.
steps: Reduced compliance means the artery wall is stiffer and cannot stretch to absorb each pulse of blood.
The heart must pump against higher pressure, so the heart muscle works harder and the blood pressure rises (hypertension).
High pressure and stiff walls damage the endothelium, so cholesterol and fibrous plaque can build up (atherosclerosis).
Plaques narrow the lumen and can block the artery, causing heart attack or stroke.

questions.answer: About 60.7 beats per minute (from about 69.8 to about 130.4 beats per minute).

Increase = 130.43 - 69.77 = 60.7 beats per minute.

questions.question: Which molecule, released from platelets, results in blood clotting? Options: A fibrinogen, B prothrombin, C thrombin, D thromboplastin.
questions.answer: D thromboplastin.
steps: Platelets release thromboplastin when the vessel is damaged.
Thromboplastin converts prothrombin into thrombin, which starts the clotting cascade.
Fibrinogen, prothrombin and thrombin are plasma proteins, not stored in platelets, so A, B and C are wrong.
Platelets release thromboplastin at the site of damage.

questions.question: Which pair of molecules are enzymes in their active form? Options: A fibrinogen and prothrombin, B prothrombin and thrombin, C thrombin and thromboplastin, D thromboplastin and prothrombin.
questions.answer: C thrombin and thromboplastin.
steps: Thrombin is an active enzyme.
Thromboplastin is an active enzyme that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
Prothrombin and fibrinogen are inactive precursors, so options A, B and D are wrong.
Thrombin and thromboplastin are both active enzymes in the clotting pathway.

questions.question: Which molecule found in the blood is insoluble? Options: A fibrin, B fibrinogen, C prothrombin, D thromboplastin.
questions.answer: A fibrin.
steps: Fibrinogen is a soluble plasma protein.
Fibrin is formed from fibrinogen as insoluble threads that make up the clot mesh.
Prothrombin and thromboplastin are not insoluble plasma components in this context, so the answer is A.
Insoluble fibrin is the protein that forms the solid part of the clot.

questions.question: Suggest why a pulmonary embolism, where a clot blocks the pulmonary artery, can cause difficulty in breathing and a rapid heart rate.
questions.answer: The clot blocks blood flow to the lungs, so less gas exchange occurs; the body senses low oxygen and breathes faster while the heart beats faster to try to keep oxygen delivery up.
steps: A clot in the pulmonary artery blocks blood flow to part of the lungs.
Less blood reaches the alveoli, so less oxygen enters the blood and less carbon dioxide is removed.
Low blood oxygen and high carbon dioxide are detected by chemoreceptors, causing faster breathing and a sense of breathlessness.
The heart beats faster to keep the delivery of oxygen to the body cells as high as possible.

questions.question: Discuss whether the finding that hibernating bears produce less HSP47, a protein that binds platelets to damaged vessels, could be useful to humans.
questions.answer: It could help develop drugs that reduce platelet binding to lower the risk of DVT, but the balance matters because platelets must still seal real wounds, so more research is needed.
steps: HSP47 helps platelets bind to damaged blood vessels, which is part of clot formation.
Bears with less HSP47 may form fewer clots during inactivity, which suggests a target for drugs against DVT.
Reducing binding too much could increase bleeding from wounds, so the effect must be controlled carefully.
The finding needs testing in humans before any treatment could be developed.

questions.question: Complete the passage about prothrombin: it is transported in the plasma of a human; it is converted into thrombin by an enzyme; the substrate for thrombin is a named molecule.
questions.answer: Plasma; thromboplastin (prothrombin activator); fibrinogen.
steps: Prothrombin is a soluble protein carried in the blood plasma.
Thromboplastin (prothrombin activator) converts prothrombin into the active enzyme thrombin.
Thrombin acts as an enzyme on its substrate fibrinogen, converting it into insoluble fibrin.
Prothrombin is converted into thrombin with the help of thromboplastin and calcium ions.

questions.question: Which pair of drugs is used to treat patients who have short blood clotting times? Options: A anticoagulants and antihypertensives, B anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors, C antihypertensives and statins, D platelet inhibitors and statins.
questions.answer: B anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors.
steps: A short clotting time means the blood clots too easily, so clotting must be slowed.
Anticoagulants slow the clotting cascade (e.g. heparin).
Platelet inhibitors stop platelets clumping together (e.g. aspirin).
Antihypertensives and statins do not directly reduce clotting, so answer B is correct.

questions.question: A person with a prothrombin time (PT) of 8.5 seconds was treated to increase it to 10 seconds. Calculate the percentage increase in PT.
questions.answer: 17.6 % (to 1 decimal place).
steps: Increase = 10 - 8.5 = 1.5 seconds.
Percentage increase = (1.5 / 8.5) x 100.
1.5 / 8.5 = 0.1765, so the percentage increase is 17.6 %.
Percentage increase is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100.

questions.question: Which describes the sketched oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin? Options: A linear curve showing a positive correlation, B linear curve showing a negative correlation, C sigmoid curve showing a negative correlation, D sigmoid curve showing a positive correlation.
questions.answer: D sigmoid curve showing a positive correlation.
steps: The oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin is S-shaped (sigmoid), not a straight line.
Saturation rises as partial pressure of oxygen rises, so the correlation is positive.
Option D correctly gives a sigmoid curve with positive correlation.
The sigmoid shape reflects cooperative binding of oxygen to haemoglobin.

questions.question: Which name is given to the effect of increasing carbon dioxide concentration on the dissociation curve? Options: A Benedict, B Bohr, C Fick, D Stahl.
questions.answer: B Bohr.
steps: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
This shifts the dissociation curve to the right, so more oxygen is released to respiring tissues.
This effect is called the Bohr effect, so the answer is B.
The Bohr effect lowers affinity when CO2 is high, which helps oxygen release in respiring tissues.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of haemoglobin is related to its function in transporting oxygen and carbon dioxide.
questions.answer: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains each with a haem group containing iron that binds oxygen reversibly, and its globin chains bind carbon dioxide, which reduces oxygen affinity.
steps: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains (quaternary structure), each with a haem group.
Each haem group contains an iron ion (Fe2+), which binds one oxygen molecule reversibly.
Oxygen binding is cooperative, so binding at one site makes it easier to bind at the next.
Carbon dioxide binds to the globin chains (and affects their shape), lowering oxygen affinity so oxygen is released to respiring tissues.
